title: FX option expiries for 11 September 10am New York cut
body: USD/JPY: 154.00 US$2.86bn 153.00 US$2.74bn 152.00 US$1.66bn EUR/USD: 1.1575 EUR1.44bn 1.1600 EUR996.2mn 1.1500 EUR947mn AUD/USD: 0.7150 AUD657.4mn 0.7250 AUD622.1mn 0.7110 AUD543.5mn USD/CAD: 1.3900 US$693.8mn 1.3800 US$535mn 1.3950 US$319.7mn GBP/USD: 1.3630 GBP565.4mn 1.3500 GBP540mn Q&A: FX option expiries What exactly is an FX option expiry? An FX option gives its holder the right, though not the requirement, to buy or sell one currency for another at an agreed rate, called the strike, on or before a set date. That date is the expiry. Why can a large expiry influence the spot market? It largely comes down to hedging. Banks and dealers who have written these options typically hedge their exposure by trading the underlying currency pair. As spot price approaches the strike, those hedges often need adjusting, which can generate extra buying or selling in the spot market. Does a large expiry automatically mean price will move towards the strike? Not necessarily, and this is worth remembering. An expiry is context, not a signal. Say EUR/USD sits at 1.1600 with a large expiry at 1.1800: that expiry likely won't have much sway on its own. But if EUR/USD is trading at 1.1790 with only a few hours left before the option lapses, the strike becomes far more relevant to price action. title: FARTCOIN selloff - Here's what most traders miss about 'exchange inflow' selling signals
body: FARTCOIN's reported 20 percent slide over 24 hours, alongside more than 6.5 million tokens moving to exchange hot wallets, is a useful live example of a pattern that recurs across crypto markets whenever a price move coincides with an on-chain transfer story. The transfers themselves, including flows attributed to Coinbase Prime Custody, Gate.io and market maker Wintermute, are drawn from a single on-chain tracking account rather than confirmed by the exchanges or custodians involved, and a transfer to an exchange wallet is not the same event as an executed sale. Even the reporting's own netflow figures showed inflows only modestly ahead of outflows on the day, smaller than some earlier periods, which sits awkwardly against headline framing built around the 6.5 million figure alone. For traders, the practical takeaway extends well beyond this one token: exchange inflow data is a probability shift, not a confirmed sell order, and treating it as the latter risks overstating both the certainty and the size of the pressure implied. --- FARTCOIN's latest slide is a good case study in why 'tokens moved to exchanges' headlines deserve a second look before they're read as confirmed selling.
